The detection sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is significantly limited by the movement of their mirrors in response to high-frequency gravitational waves. To address this issue, we propose a novel design called the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which uses two masses connected by a spring to form an anti-parallel oscillator system. This design allows the masses to move in opposite directions, effectively increasing the displacement caused by gravitational waves and enhancing the detection sensitivity. We demonstrate that this new design can be integrated into existing detection systems without any major modifications, and we also propose a modified readout scheme called the dual-shearing Mach-Zehnder interferometer to fully utilize the increased detection range. This new design and readout scheme can be used to improve the high-frequency detection capabilities of current gravitational wave detectors without any major modifications.

In multi-user wireless networks, users' transmission areas can overlap, leading to interference and reduced data rates. This paper proposes a novel approach to eliminate overlapping transmission areas by utilizing a stochastic access protocol and advanced beamforming techniques in wireless systems with a vast number of antennas. The approach is modeled as a stochastic geometry problem, and its performance is analyzed using mathematical formulas. The results show that the proposed method can effectively prevent transmission area overlap, leading to improved data rates and reduced interference. The approach is also flexible and can be adapted to different system configurations.

A theoretical model has been developed to predict submillimeter continuum images, taking into account a key factor - vertical shear-driven migration of dust - in a range of protoplanetary disk models. The model was applied to 100 disk models, revealing that the predicted images are strongly influenced by the size and location of large dust particles, rather than small grains. The size distribution of large dust particles significantly impacts the predicted images, with different distributions resulting in varying levels of submillimeter emission and spatial patterns. The location of large dust particles also plays a crucial role, with particles trapped at pressure bumps or edges of gaps producing detectable submillimeter emission, while particles in the disk midplane produce little to no detectable emission. The model provides empirical guidelines for predicting submillimeter emission from large dust particles in protoplanetary disks, which can be used to interpret observations and infer the physical processes responsible for planet formation.

A new type of three-body force, dubbed big apple, has been developed to enhance the accuracy of nuclear forces at short distances. This big apple force is based on interactions between three nucleons and involves two delta resonances and one nucleon, mediated by two pion exchanges and one single-pion emission. We incorporated this big apple force into the Brueckner-Hartree-Fock framework to investigate finite nuclei, and found that it significantly impacts the saturation properties of nuclear matter. Specifically, adjusting the parameters of this force allows us to successfully describe the saturation properties of symmetric nuclear matter, as well as the symmetry energy and its slope at saturation density. Additionally, this force has significant implications for the density profiles and symmetry energy of neutron stars.

This research develops a robust quantum logic gate for trapped ions that relies on an isotropic interaction and is resistant to frequency detuning errors. By utilizing an interaction that is intraharmonic and isotropic, we demonstrate that a Molmer-Sorensen gate can be implemented with high fidelity, even in the presence of significant frequency detuning errors. Our study shows that a 1000-qubit chain of calcium ions can be operated with an error rate of 0.1% per gate, and that a 100-qubit chain can be operated with an average error rate of 0.1% per gate. Furthermore, we propose a method for an isotropic, intraharmonic interaction that is insensitive to second-order frequency shifts, and find that a 1000-qubit chain can be operated with an average error rate of 10^-4 per gate.

We develop a framework to investigate the impact of a Hubbard U on a Dirac material with linear dispersion near the K and K' points. In our approach, we incorporate a large U into the tight-binding model for graphene and construct a Green's function to derive an effective Hamiltonian. This allows us to examine the effects of a large U on graphene's electronic structure, including the emergence of a Mott-Hubbard gap and the formation of flat bands. Furthermore, we explore how a large U affects the topological properties of graphene, including the emergence of a Chern-Simons term and the formation of a topological insulator phase.

The search for new, massive neutral leptons is a key area of investigation in lepton universality studies. By analyzing 10^12 kaon-plus decays into neutral pion, electron, and new neutral lepton combinations, the NA62 experiment at CERN aims to significantly improve current limits on new interaction strengths. This study outlines the expected improvements in sensitivity for various theoretical models, including those based on effective field theory and extensions to the standard model, and demonstrates the ability to detect or rule out new, massive neutral leptons with masses up to 335 MeV.

Neural language models have largely surpassed traditional $n$-gram models in recent years. However, their high computational costs and reduced efficiency in leveraging existing $n$-gram models have become apparent. In this study, we introduce a novel approach that combines the strengths of both technologies. By training a neural network to predict the residual probability between an $n$-gram model and the true probability distribution, we can achieve comparable performance to standalone neural models while significantly reducing computational costs and enabling the use of efficient $n$-gram models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by training it on a Wikipedia corpus and evaluating it on the Penn Treebank, achieving a perplexity of 81.1 with a smaller 2-gram model and 70.4 with a larger 4-gram model. We also explore the benefits of this method for text generation, particularly in low-resource settings where pre-trained $n$-gram models can be fine-tuned for specific domains.

To address the challenges of accurately predicting 3D face landmarks in highly occluded and diverse faces, we have developed a novel end-to-end framework called SADRNet. This framework combines two complementary sub-networks, each responsible for a distinct aspect of face analysis. The first sub-network, named the Global Face Reconstruction Network (GFRN), generates a comprehensive representation of a face by integrating multiple face images and reconstructing them. The second sub-network, the Self-Aligned Local Face Regression Network (SALFNR), is designed to predict face landmarks for individual images by leveraging the global representation generated by GFRN. To ensure the consistency of the two sub-networks, we have implemented a self-alignment mechanism that enables SALFNR to learn from GFRN's global representation. To further enhance the robustness of SALFNR, we have designed a dual face prediction strategy that trains it to handle both aligned and unaligned input images. Our experimental results on three widely used datasets, 300-W, CFP, and WFLW, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in achieving accurate face landmark prediction.

The formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) is closely linked to the early universe's inflationary period. A key theory posits that a small-scale power spectrum enhancement caused by an oscillating inflaton field could lead to PBH formation. In this study, we investigate the possibility of PBH formation resulting from a sudden change in a power-law inflaton field, which creates a scalar curvature perturbation. We find that this scenario does not lead to PBH formation, as it generates a long-wavelength curvature perturbation rather than the required local overdensity. However, we demonstrate that introducing an $\alpha$-attractor model with an oscillating mass term can result in PBH formation by generating a local density perturbation. We also explore the possibility of a hybrid inflation model that combines an $\alpha$-attractor and a monomial potential, which could lead to PBH formation.

A labeled ordered tree with n nodes is a structure consisting of n distinct elements arranged in a specific order and forming a tree-like pattern. The set of deepest nodes in such a structure forms a connected subgraph with the minimum possible number of edges, which is equal to the distance between the furthest apart deepest nodes. The number of labeled ordered trees with n nodes where the deepest nodes are arranged in a line is (n!)/(2^a) times the product of the sizes of its node clusters, where a represents the number of cluster sizes that appear more than once. Additionally, the generating function for these types of trees can be expressed as a power series in x, where the coefficient of x^a represents the sum of the products of the sizes of its node clusters for all trees with n nodes.

A data integrity system is essential for preserving the trust in elections.  To enhance this system, we developed iOCR, an informed OCR tool specifically designed to verify tabulated election results.  Unlike traditional OCR tools, iOCR leverages the known structure of election result tables to improve accuracy and efficiency.  By incorporating informed constraints, iOCR can correct common OCR errors and validate the accuracy of scanned ballots.  We tested iOCR on real election ballots and found it to be significantly more accurate than state-of-the-art OCR tools, with a 99.9% accuracy rate.  iOCR can be easily adapted to various ballot formats and provides a foundation for further research into informed data entry systems.

We investigate the implications of over-parameterization in a linear regression model with time series data, including noise and varying coefficients. Our research reveals that when the model is highly over-parameterized, the time-varying components of the model can be accurately estimated, leading to improved performance compared to a static model. In contrast, when the model is not over-parameterized, the performance is comparable to the static model. These findings are supported by theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

In this work, a stochastic storage management problem is investigated for a solitary
energy storage system operating within decentralized markets characterized by uncertainty.
Rather than relying on traditional approaches, we apply cautious decision-making principles
to formulate an optimal control framework. This framework results in a stochastic dynamic
programming equation that can be resolved through an iterative policy evaluation and
improvement process. Notably, both the value function and the corresponding policy
function exhibit convex properties, allowing for an efficient and accelerated solution
methodology. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of our approach to a storage
system operating within an electricity market, with numerical simulations providing
supportive evidence.

A numerical experiment was conducted to investigate the relationship between the temperature differences between the equator and the poles and the atmospheric circulation patterns on a planet with fixed conditions at the equator and poles but varying radiative cooling at mid-latitudes. The results showed that the atmospheric circulation patterns changed from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence as the temperature difference increased. The transition between these patterns was found to be abrupt and sudden, rather than gradual. The study also found that the patterns were symmetric and stable, with little variation over time. The results were found to be consistent with previous research on the relationship between temperature differences and atmospheric circulation patterns. The research was carried out using a simplified model of atmospheric circulation, with the goal of gaining a better understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that drive atmospheric patterns on planets.

We investigate the effectiveness of dynamic learning rate and batch size
adjustments during neural network training, particularly in large-scale
computer vision applications. Our study reveals that this adaptive approach
outperforms static learning strategies, especially when dealing with large
datasets and batch sizes. Notably, our method enables the successful
training of a ResNet-101 model on ImageNet with a batch size of 4096,
achieving a top-1 accuracy of 80.1%. This performance surpasses the previous
best result obtained with the same model and batch size, which had a top-1
accuracy of 79.8%.

Researchers have developed a comprehensive multi-valley effective mass model to accurately simulate the quantum states of three exchange-coupled donor impurities in silicon. This enhanced model includes detailed multi-valley corrections and is validated against a configuration interaction approach across all possible orbital and spin states. The study reveals that neglecting multi-valley corrections can lead to significant errors in estimating the effective Hamiltonian, particularly in specific orbital states. Notably, the model predicts that the effective Hamiltonian can be inaccurate by up to 1.2 mK for certain three-donor states, and that the coupling between the outer two donors can be significantly affected, with an error of up to 10% compared to the inner two. The model's accuracy is demonstrated through the calculation of the He-3-singlet-triplet splitting and the double-quantum transition frequency for a linear chain of three-donors, with an error of less than 0.1 micro-electron volt. The model's efficiency is highlighted by its ability to calculate the energy spectrum of a linear chain of three-donors with 100 different positions in less than 0.1 seconds.

Our study examines the quantum conduction properties of HgTe quantum wells situated within their gapless phase, specifically focusing on the (111) and (110) crystallographic planes. We have developed a comprehensive analytical framework to examine the influence of interface roughness on the conduction of these quantum wells. Our findings reveal that the (111) plane exhibits significantly stronger scattering effects compared to the (110) plane, as a result of the unique nature of Dirac particle interactions. This distinction is further highlighted by the observation that the mobility of the (111) plane is approximately an order of magnitude lower than that of the (110) plane. Furthermore, we have established a direct correlation between the Dirac point location and the roughness of the interface, providing a means to precisely predict the location of the Dirac point based on the characteristics of the interface.

This research paper focuses on optimizing the uplink and downlink time slots in TDD systems to maximize network throughput. We developed a framework that uses a Nash Equilibrium to determine the best scheduling for TDD systems, considering the constraints of adjacent frequency bands. Our approach allows for a flexible configuration of TDD systems, where each frequency band can independently choose its scheduling and uplink or downlink orientation. This method is particularly useful for managing the limited spectrum resources in 5G networks. To test our framework, we conducted simulations that showed the effectiveness of our approach in maximizing network throughput.

Reinforcement learning methods that rely on policy gradients have achieved significant success in various domains, but they require a computationally expensive calculation of task dynamics during the gradient estimation process. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that enables the direct learning of dynamics gradients through a neural network based on Hamilton's principle. This innovation allows for the seamless integration of our method with existing reinforcement learning frameworks, such as actor-critic architectures, without any additional computational overhead during the estimation of policy gradients. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through comprehensive experiments on both continuous and discrete control tasks, demonstrating its ability to enhance the performance of baseline models.

A proposed framework for developing trustworthy machine learning models incorporates a component that involves a human in the process, specifically a data augmentation method that leverages the preferences of a human to improve a model's reliability. This approach focuses on a specific aspect of artificial intelligence research, emphasizing the importance of creating trustworthy models rather than just accurate ones. The framework is comprised of three main parts, including a supervised environment where an agent interacts with a user, a method for selecting data that maximizes the influence of a human's preferences, and evaluations using real-world datasets to assess the effectiveness of this approach. The results demonstrate that this data augmentation method produces models that are more reliable according to the ratings of a human user, and also more accurate than models created using traditional methods for selecting data.

We develop a new quantum invariant for links within the thickened torus, denoted as $F_2^L$, which is inspired by the invariant originally created by Goussarov, Habiro, and Murakami for knots and links in three-dimensional space. This new invariant exhibits the volume conjecture property, mirroring the distinctive characteristics of the Kauffman invariant in the same space. Furthermore, we establish that our invariant is equivalent to the Kauffman invariant when the latter is defined with specific parameters.

To enhance word sense disambiguation, a method is proposed that leverages contextual information to differentiate between multiple meanings of ambiguous words. This approach utilizes a context-sensitive graph to identify and eliminate incorrect word sense interpretations by analyzing the context of surrounding words. A key aspect of this model is the use of context-gloss vectors, which are derived from a context-aware word2vec framework and integrated into traditional disambiguation models. This context-gloss integration aims to improve the accuracy of word sense selection by incorporating a deeper understanding of the target word's context. Experimental results on the SemEval 2013 task demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that it outperforms a baseline model and achieves a significant improvement in word sense disambiguation.

This study provides a fresh proof of the fundamental properties of the reciprocal Gamma function, denoted as $1/\Gamma(z)$, utilizing its integral representation. We derive a set of integral formulas for $1/\Gamma(z)$ that are similar to those previously established by G. S. Tarry in 1925. Furthermore, we establish new relationships between these integral expressions and the Bessel function of the first kind, $J_0$.

A theoretical investigation has been conducted to analyze the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 50 TeV, focusing on the gluon distribution within the nucleus. The study employs various gluon distribution models to predict top quark production cross sections for proton-nucleus and top-quark-initiated semi-exclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS) processes. The results indicate that top quark-initiated SIDIS could be observable in future electron-ion colliders, particularly with high-luminosity electron beams. The study also explores top quark-initiated SIDIS in the context of exclusive and semi-exclusive processes, where the final state top quark is detected and the proton or nucleus remains intact. The study finds that top quark-initiated SIDIS with intact beams is unlikely to be observed due to the low cross sections for diffractive deep inelastic scattering (DISS) at high-x values. The study also compares top quark production in proton-nucleus and proton-proton collisions, finding that top quark production in proton-proton collisions is expected to be the dominant process at LHC energies. The study also discusses the top quark-initiated SIDIS cross sections for different collision energies and the implications for future experiments.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing aims to automatically convert natural language queries into SQL based on a given database schema. Existing research primarily focuses on single-domain scenarios, but text-to-SQL systems developed for single domains struggle when applied to new domains with different schema structures. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called CDTTS, which extends text-to-SQL models to handle multiple domains effectively. CDTTS incorporates an auxiliary task that learns the relationship between natural language and schema information, enabling the model to generalize across domains. Experimental results on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of CDTTS over baseline methods in terms of execution accuracy and exact set matching.

This paper explores the concept of differential privacy within graph-based data, providing a comprehensive analysis of existing research and potential applications. We begin by defining key terms and outlining fundamental properties of graphs, then proceed to examine various approaches to defining inputs for the purpose of differential privacy analysis. Our investigation reveals that traditional DP properties are insufficient to fully capture the essence of privacy preservation in graph data, leading us to propose a more suitable framework for evaluating privacy guarantees. We also discuss the implications of our findings for both theoretical research and practical applications, particularly in the context of machine learning and data mining. Our work is intended to serve as a foundation for further investigation into the use of graph data in privacy-preserving analytics.

The next generation of large-scale surveys for optical and near-infrared astronomy will be led by the Euclid space telescope. This ambitious project builds upon the foundations established by previous initiatives such as the SDSS, DESI, 4MOST, and DES. The Euclid's unprecedented capabilities in imaging and spectroscopy over vast areas of the sky will unlock new possibilities for studying the evolution of galaxies, the physical processes that drive star formation, and the supermassive black holes at the center of galaxies. The in-depth analysis of Euclid's data will require the development of sophisticated observational techniques and infrastructure, which will be made available to the scientific community through innovative observational programs. The paper outlines the cutting-edge research areas that will be explored through these inherited science opportunities, which will be made possible through the collaboration between astronomers and the Euclid mission.

A new approach called the phase-space random quantum hydrodynamics (PS-RQHD) has been developed to model the dynamics of a two-dimensional interacting Bose fluid. This approach uses a stochastic mean-field theory based on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, where the initial mean field is perturbed by white noise. By employing the cumulant expansion, an infinite set of hydrodynamic equations is derived, which can be simplified to a finite set of closed equations under the second-order cumulant approximation. Numerical simulations using a finite-difference time-domain method demonstrate that PS-RQHD accurately replicates the dynamics of a Bose fluid in the absence of rotation and can also model the behavior of a rotating Bose fluid.

This research paper examines the conditions under which the probability of a specific event, defined as the sum of a sequence of letters exceeding a certain threshold, is significantly lower than expected. The study focuses on the impact of the correlation between letters on the probability of such events, and derives an expression for the probability of exceeding a threshold for a first-order Markov chain. The paper also compares the results to those obtained from independent and identically distributed letter sequences, and presents both numerical and analytical findings.

Let M, N be non-empty, disjoint, closed subsets of a metric space X. Define C(X; M, N) as the collection of all continuous functions from X to the unit interval that are 1 at points in M and 0 at points in N. For any function ρ within C(X; M, N), we identify a homotopy class [ρ] consisting of functions equivalent to ρ under continuous deformations preserving the boundary conditions on ∂X. Within each homotopy class [ρ], we find functions ρ̄ that minimize the integral of ρ over X. The collection of points in X where these minimizing functions ρ̄ are greater than zero forms a region Ω̄. We investigate the topological properties of Ω̄, demonstrating that it consistently exhibits the same topological structure across all minimizing regions Ω̄ within a given homotopy class [ρ]. Additionally, we establish the existence of a continuous deformation that preserves the boundary conditions and transforms any given function ρ̄ into a harmonic function on Ω̄.

A detailed analysis of Ni isotopes from 58Ni to 78Ni was conducted, focusing on their low-lying, zero-spin energy states. This examination revealed a significant lack of research on Ni isotopes between 64Ni and 70Ni, with 64Ni being particularly intriguing due to its multiple zero-spin, zero-angular momentum states. Various theoretical models were applied to examine the characteristics of 64Ni, including collective rotation, vibration, and shell structure, along with their interplay. The study found that the coexistence of two nuclear structures in 64Ni can be attributed to the tensor force, with one state belonging to the g-p shell and another to the f-p shell. A proposed double-particle hole configuration was found to align with the observed state in 64Ni.

We introduce J-K fold cross validation, an extension of traditional k fold cross validation, which divides data into j distinct subsets, each consisting of k non-overlapping folds. This method allows for the training and testing of a model j times using different combinations of training and test sets. We evaluate the J-K fold method's effectiveness in improving the performance of various NLP models, including a logistic regression classifier, BERT, and GPT-2, across multiple sentiment analysis and question answering tasks. Our findings indicate that J-K fold cross validation can significantly reduce variance when tuning hyperparameters and training NLP models. We also provide an open-source implementation of our method at https://github.com/andrewjw/JKfoldCV.

Reinforcement learning has been extensively researched and applied in recent years. A significant breakthrough in this field is the concept of "educators-pupils" framework, which divides the learning process into two stages: an educator acquires knowledge through interaction with the environment, and a pupil learns from the educator's knowledge. This framework has been particularly effective in complex learning tasks, such as playing Go, where a pupil learns from a relatively small amount of data generated by an educator. This paper provides an overview of the educator-pupils framework, covering various learning methods used by educators and pupils, as well as the exchange of knowledge between them. It also covers recent developments in this area, including the use of generative models, multi-pupil learning, and the integration of supervised learning.

The factor graph framework, initially proposed by Kschischang et al. in 2001, serves a purpose similar to that of graphical models, providing a more comprehensive representation. This framework represents relationships between variables and factors through binary edges, which can be useful for certain analyses. Building on this foundation, our research focuses on refining the algorithmic depiction of functions within graphical models, as presented in our paper. This enhanced representation can facilitate a clearer understanding of key properties, such as the size of the smallest space required to accurately describe specific relationships within the model. We also demonstrate how this representation can be utilized to derive an exact, polynomial-time algorithm for computing the most probable configuration under local constraints, as defined in each clique of the model. This approach significantly outperforms existing methods, reducing the computational complexity from an exponential to a linear exponential function of the model's treewidth. Furthermore, our algorithmic representation provides a more intuitive explanation for the connection between two well-known approximation methods, namely the loopy Belief Propagation and the Min-Sum algorithm, in relation to finding the most probable configuration within the model.

The behavior of suspensions experiencing shear stress varies significantly, either maintaining a smooth flow or undergoing a sudden transition to a turbulent state. This phenomenon, known as shear thickening, has been extensively studied in recent years, particularly focusing on the effects of particle size, density, and volume fraction. Researchers have found that these variables influence the onset of shear thickening, but not in a uniform manner. By incorporating the effects of surface area and friction, a universal scaling law has been developed to describe the onset of shear thickening across different densities and friction coefficients. This universal scaling law highlights the fundamental role of particle surface area in driving the onset of shear thickening.

A significant amount of online information is irrelevant to users, and this issue is compounded by the personalization of search engines, which can inadvertently prevent users from encountering diverse viewpoints. This study investigates the extent of information that users may overlook when relying on Google Web Search, specifically examining whether users can be made aware of information that is available but inaccessible to them. The findings reveal that users are unable to independently discover information that is present but not accessible to them, and this inability is linked to the personalization of search engines. The study also provides a theoretical framework for understanding the limitations of human information processing and the impact of search engine personalization on users' exposure to diverse information.

This paper outlines the potential for a new synchrotron, the $\mu$C1000, designed to accelerate muons at the CERN facility. The proposed design enables a synchrotron capable of reaching 1 TeV with a 500-meter circumference, providing a platform for high-luminosity fixed-target and muon collider experiments. Calculated luminosity values for both fixed-target and 10 TeV collider scenarios demonstrate the benefits of the $\mu$C1000 over current and planned facilities. The paper also outlines key technical challenges and potential solutions for developing the $\mu$C1000, including necessary upgrades to existing CERN infrastructure.

We have developed a novel MRI sequence that utilizes a modified 4D TSE/TurboSpinEcho technique to provide high-quality, three-dimensional images corrected for motion, suitable for a wide range of clinical applications. This sequence is capable of producing images from patients who are not able to hold their breath or lie still during the scan, which is common in many clinical scenarios. We have optimized the sequence to produce high-quality images with a short scan time, low noise, and minimal motion artifacts. Our results show that this sequence provides clear anatomical detail and can accurately identify abnormalities in various body parts, including the liver, kidneys, pancreas, spleen, and lymph nodes. This sequence has been successfully used to identify abnormalities in multiple patients with various conditions, including liver cancer, kidney cancer, and lymph node enlargement. Our findings suggest that this sequence is a valuable tool for clinical use, providing high-quality, motion-corrected images that can be used for diagnosis and treatment planning.

In statistical hypothesis testing, particularly when using nonparametric methods, the choice of a suitable p-value calculation method is crucial. Paired-permutation tests are widely used for calculating p-values, but their efficiency and accuracy can vary significantly depending on the specific structured testing scenario. This study investigates the impact of data characteristics on the performance of different paired-permutation examination methods, specifically focusing on the relationship between data distribution and the effectiveness of various examination strategies. A novel Precise Paired-Permutation (PPP) approach is proposed to address these challenges, and its superiority over existing methods is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and extensive simulations. The PPP approach is also applied to a real-world dataset, showcasing its practical relevance. The findings of this study have significant implications for the accurate calculation of p-values in nonparametric testing, and they contribute to the development of more efficient and reliable statistical examination methods.

This research presents a comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping volumes, new container prices, secondhand container prices, and scrap container prices from 1966 to 2019, sourced from official publications and industry reports. By combining these data, we can examine the long-term trends in the container shipping industry. Our analysis reveals that real freight rates and shipping volumes experienced significant growth in the 1970s, but have been declining since the 1990s. We also found that new and secondhand container prices have been consistently rising in the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, but have been declining since the 2000s. Furthermore, we found that real shipping volumes are positively correlated with freight rates, new and secondhand container prices, but are negatively correlated with scrap container prices. We believe this unified dataset can be valuable for future studies on the container shipping industry.

The concept of fabric spaces is introduced, which are directed spaces that can be given a topological structure by assigning a simplicial complex. This complex is defined by a set of simplicial morphisms that preserve ordering and maintain specific properties. It is shown that the 2-sphere can be given a fabric space structure, which allows for a connection to the problem of the Higgs field in the 2D Abelian Higgs model. This model is then reformulated in terms of a U(1) gauge theory on the simplicial complex, which is given a specific structure by a map to the category of vector spaces. This reformulation is equivalent to the original model, which is then studied using the path integral approach. This approach is given a specific formulation by a sum over changing simplicial complexes, which is defined by a map to the category of simplicial complexes. This formulation is then compared to the standard path integral approach, which is given a specific formulation by a sum over triangulations of a fixed manifold. This standard approach is then reformulated in terms of a U(1) gauge theory on a fixed manifold, which is given a specific structure by a map to the category of vector bundles. This reformulation is then studied using the heat kernel approach, which is given a specific formulation by a sum over eigenvalues of the Laplacian operator. This paper proposes a two-fold approach to address the challenge of generating
synthetic data that maintains the statistical properties of real data while
capturing complex non-linear relationships. We combine the predictive
capabilities of a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)
model with the data generation capabilities of a Variational Adversarial Network
(VAEGAN) framework. The results show that our hybrid model outperforms
traditional forecasting methods, including ARIMA and LSTM, in terms of
forecasting accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate that our model generates
high-quality synthetic data that is indistinguishable from real data. Our
research contributes to the growing body of literature on financial forecasting
and generative modeling, and has practical implications for a range of
applications, including fraud detection and data augmentation.

We investigated the double Higgs boson production process at future TeV-scale electron-positron colliders, specifically the ILC and CLIC, to determine the maximum precision achievable in measuring BSM Higgs boson couplings. Using a type-III two-Higgs doublet model as an example, we focused on the coupling between the Higgs bosons and vector bosons. We found that for a model with no electroweak doublet doublet coupling, the ILC could reach a 10% precision in measuring this coupling at 250 GeV center-of-mass energy with 2 ab^-1 of data, and the CLIC could reach a 5% precision at 3 TeV center-of-mass energy with 3 ab^-1 of data. However, for a model with a non-zero electroweak doublet doublet coupling, the precision achievable is significantly worse, with the ILC and CLIC reaching precisions of 100% and 50% respectively. We also found that the double Higgs production process is sensitive to a wide range of new physics models beyond the Standard Model.

We have developed a covariant Hamiltonian formalism for the classical theory of gravity, which is based on the geodesic equation, and have examined three classical gravity theories that feature second-order geodesic equations. These theories are known as Einstein gravity, Nordtvedic gravity, and Fock's gravity. We have found that Einstein gravity and Nordtvedic gravity are equivalent, and have also discovered that they share the same number of physical degrees of freedom. We have also found that Fock's gravity is not equivalent to Einstein gravity, and have shown that it has a much larger symmetry group than Einstein gravity.

We investigated the anisotropic drag coefficients of cylinders with varying aspect ratios and surface roughness, placed between layers of sand. Cylinders were used to represent cylindrical voids found in geology, and their drag anisotropy was found to be influenced by their shape and surface texture. Our research showed that the relationship between the drag coefficients and the cylinders' orientation was affected by their aspect ratios and roughness, and that this anisotropy could be used to understand the properties of sedimentary rocks.

Our study utilizes the multiphase transport model to examine the evolution of quark-gluon plasma in 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions, focusing on the calculation of elliptic and triangular flow coefficients, $v_2$ and $v_2\langle\langle n_\phi\rangle\rangle$, as well as the initial particle number multiplicity, $n$. By incorporating thermal fluctuations into the initial state, we find that $v_2\langle\langle n_\phi\rangle\rangle$ and $n$ are influenced by the thermal fluctuation strength, whereas $v_2$ remains unaffected. Furthermore, we find that $v_3$ and $v_3\langle\langle n_\phi\rangle\rangle$ are independent of the thermal fluctuation strength. However, we find that $v_2$ and $v_3$ are strongly correlated, whereas $n_\phi$ is more closely linked to $v_2\langle\langle n_\phi\rangle\rangle$ and $n$. Additionally, we find that $n_\phi$ is more closely correlated with $v_2$ than $v_3$.

This article summarizes selected ATLAS experiments that probe the unusual aspects of the Standard Model, specifically focusing on two areas: rare decay processes and the production of electrically neutral Higgs bosons in association with beauty quarks. In addition, it outlines forthcoming ATLAS investigations of beauty quark decays, which could potentially reveal deviations from the Standard Model.

This study aims to develop a theoretical framework for applying iterative methods to discretized partial differential equation systems that preserve key physical properties. We specifically focus on linear systems resulting from finite element discretizations of second-order elliptic problems using $H(\text{curl},\Omega)$-conforming elements. To address these systems, we propose a new approach that combines a simple, modified physical preconditioner with two iterative solvers: the conjugate gradient method and the preconditioned restricted additive Schwarz algorithm. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms.

This research introduces a novel, flexible volume-to-surface registration method that leverages a biomechanical model of the hand. Unlike previous approaches, our model accounts for the varying stiffness of hand tissues, which is crucial for accurate registration. To represent this variability, we developed a hybrid parameterization of the biomechanical model that combines discrete and continuous parameters. This allows for efficient and scalable model parameterization, which is essential for real-time applications. Our approach was tested on both synthetic and real hand data, demonstrating its ability to accurately align the biomechanical model with the target surface. Our results show that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of registration accuracy and computational efficiency.

3D scene flow estimation is a challenging task that involves estimating the motion of every 3D point within a scene over time. This problem is compounded by the lack of ground truth motion data in real-world settings. To overcome this limitation, self-supervised learning methods have been widely used, relying on the optical flow of two projected images to predict scene flow and then refining the estimate through reconstruction loss. However, these methods are prone to errors in areas with occlusions and motion blur. To address this issue, researchers have developed metric learning approaches that classify points as either reliable or unreliable based on their flow estimates, and adjust the network accordingly. Nevertheless, these methods are susceptible to manipulation and require the input of real-world data. In contrast, our proposed method, Self-Guided Flow, estimates the metric in the target scene's latent space and uses it to guide the network through a multi-task learning framework. We show that our approach can be trained in a self-supervised manner and outperforms existing methods on both KITTI and Sintel datasets.

This paper presents a novel approach to designing neural network classifiers that draw inspiration from biological systems, specifically by employing random neural networks in conjunction with a spiking activation function. Unlike conventional artificial neural networks, this method enables the network to classify data in an energy-efficient manner by bypassing the computation of activation functions for neurons that do not contribute to the final classification decision. To enhance the performance of this approach, we introduce a new classification algorithm that leverages the properties of the spiking random neural network. This algorithm is capable of accurately classifying data with a low error rate, while also being computationally efficient and energy-saving. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in comparison to state-of-the-art techniques, specifically by employing a subset of the network's weights for classification decision-making. This approach is shown to be both precise and energy-saving in comparison to traditional neural network classifiers.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of a spin-polarized strange quark star in the presence of a strong magnetic field at finite temperature. Using the MIT bag model, we derive the equation of state for this quark matter and determine the thermal properties of a strange quark star in the presence of a magnetic field and a specific temperature. We also calculate the critical temperature for the phase transition between hadronic and quark matter and the thermal radius and baryon number of the star. Our results show that the thermal radius and baryon number of the star increase with temperature and decrease with magnetic field strength, and that the critical temperature for the phase transition is lower in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

Let's consider a specific subcategory, denoted as $\mathcal{C}_3$, comprised of all cubic graphs. Within this framework, we define three distinct concepts: an 'ideal matching', a 'Hamiltonian circuit', and a '3-edge coloring'. Notably, we establish the following findings: first, every graph belonging to this subcategory contains at least one 'ideal matching'; second, every graph in this subcategory also includes a 'Hamiltonian circuit'; and third, for each graph in this subcategory, there exists a '3-edge coloring' that satisfies the condition that no edges of the same color form a cycle.

We introduce Timeloops, a system that leverages reinforcement learning to optimize
as call frequencies of HTTP-based microservices within a containerized
environment. By treating call frequencies as tunable parameters, Timeloops
effectively navigates the learning process, enabling it to generalize across
similar service interactions. This approach allows Timeloops to adapt to new
microservices with minimal data, a capability we refer to as transfer learning.
Our experiments, conducted on both simulated and real-world Kubernetes
environments, demonstrate that Timeloops can substantially reduce end-to-end
latency compared to random call scheduling policies.

This paper introduces a modified birth model for a multi-target filtering problem, where target locations are associated with a grid, and new targets emerge according to a probability density function within a specific region. The novel model simplifies calculations by linearizing the grid dimension, thereby reducing computational costs. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial in real-time applications, such as tracking and administration of mobile sensors, where computational efficiency is crucial. The paper also derives an updated Petersen-Roberts filter for this birth model, which is a computationally efficient approximation of the optimal filter. The proposed approach is compared to existing methods, and numerical simulations are presented to demonstrate the benefits of the modified birth model.

This study examines the null controllability of a community dynamics model featuring degeneration in a specific area. The model, originally proposed by May and Orrock, describes the evolution of a community consisting of multiple species through a system of nonlinear partial differential equations. We establish that, given a specific time frame and a limited set of species, it's possible to guide the community towards extinction in a shorter time frame by applying an appropriate control measure. Notably, our findings hold true even when the system exhibits degeneration in a particular area.

In soccer, a player's decision-making is influenced by a multitude of factors, making it a complex task to model. To address this challenge, we developed a simplified soccer game simulation that captures the essential elements of a soccer match, focusing on the choices made by a single player. Our simulation evaluates the effectiveness of different strategies by considering the dynamic interactions between players, the impact of player decisions on the game's outcome, and the influence of player decisions on the score. We then applied a reinforcement learning algorithm to optimize decision-making, and our results demonstrate that this approach can lead to significant improvements in the game's outcome. Specifically, we found that reinforcement learning can increase the number of goals scored by a player's team by up to 100% in critical game situations.

Waveform inversion is a technique used to create a detailed model of the Earth's interior by analyzing how seismic waves travel through it. A key challenge in this process is solving a nonlinear problem that arises from the relationship between the Earth's model and the observed data. To address this, researchers have developed an improved version of a method called source waveform inversion, which allows for faster and more efficient data processing. This enhanced method uses a specific type of mathematical approximation to simplify the problem, enabling the use of advanced optimization techniques. The resulting algorithm has been shown to produce accurate models of the Earth's interior in a shorter amount of time compared to previous methods. Additionally, the team has developed a new approach to model the way seismic waves spread over long distances, which further improves the quality of the resulting models.

This research investigates a two-species version of the chaotic voter model, incorporating a competition-colonization tradeoff. A novel simulation method has been developed using the GPU, enabling the modeling of extensive systems with up to 10^14 lattice sites. The study reveals that, in contrast to conventional models, the dynamics of this chaotic variant are significantly influenced by the initial conditions, resulting in a complex interplay between species elimination and coexistence.

This work considers an integrated information and energy networking (I2WN) system where a D2D link is coexisting with an ISD link, and is assisted by an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). The ISD user transmits information to the primary receiver and powers a secondary device, while the D2D user transmits information to the secondary device and harvests energy from the primary transmitter. The goal is to maximize the information rate of the D2D user by optimizing the transmit power, energy harvesting time, and phase shift of the IRS. This problem is non-convex and difficult to solve directly. To address this challenge, we develop an efficient algorithm that alternates between optimizing the transmit power, energy harvesting time, and IRS phase shift, using convex optimization techniques. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

This study presents a single-point laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) system that can perform two-dimensional velocity measurements at various locations remotely. The LDV system was programmed using LabVIEW and integrated with a 3D printed frame, a motorized stage, and a microcontroller. The system's performance was evaluated by measuring the velocity profiles of a laminar flow in a rectangular channel, and the results were compared to theoretical predictions. The study also highlights the benefits of a remotely controlled LDV system, such as its ability to perform measurements at hard-to-reach locations and its potential for use in educational settings.
Theoretical models and computer simulations have been used to assess the potential of a programmable phase disc to correct spherical aberration in a transmission electron microscope.

We provide a comprehensive analysis of the spectral and orbital stability for linearized perturbations of an anharmonic oscillator under the influence of a Klein-Gordon equation in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $d$ is either $1$ or $2$. Our study covers power-law and logarithmic non-linearities that are not too singular, non-linearity functions that are odd and growth conditions that are not too rapid. Our findings indicate that spectral and orbital stability are interconnected, and under specific conditions, orbital stability can be deduced from pointwise eigenvalue analysis of the linearized operator. Our results cover a broader range of non-linearities than previously established, including cases where the non-linearity is not smooth at the origin. Our work extends earlier research by filling gaps in the parameter space and exploring unexamined combinations of dimensions and mass function growth rates. Our analysis builds on earlier work by Dombrowski, Sereiner, and others, and provides new insights into the behavior of the Klein-Gordon equation with various non-linearities and anharmonic oscillators.

We establish a non-commutive version of Leopoldt's theorem for the rational numbers by analyzing Green's skew group ring R, which incorporates a finite abelian extension of the rationals. This involves proving that the torsion free rank of K-n cycles for R matches that of the original rational structure. Additionally, we develop a non-commutative generalization of Iwasawa's class number formula for skew group rings, which is essential for proving the cycle rank conservation law.

The Belle II experiment at KEKB is set to collect approximately 10 times more data than its predecessor, the Belle experiment, which has already produced an estimated 400 thousand signals from the decay of B mesons into muons and axion-like particles (ALPs). This abundance of data allows for a comprehensive search of rare and unconventional ALP interactions, even those with extremely low probabilities of occurring, down to $10^{-9}$, by examining the decay of B mesons into $\tau$ leptons and ALPs. A novel statistical method is also proposed to detect ALPs produced in the decay of B mesons into $\tau$ leptons and ALPs, despite their potential to be undetached, with probabilities as low as $10^{-6}$, by utilizing the existing Belle II dataset.

This paper investigates semantic shifts in words using word embeddings and evaluates various contextualized language models, including BERT, GLoVe, and FastText. By applying the Change Vector Hypothesis (CVH), we examine how shifts in a word's meaning over time affect its representation in high-dimensional space. Our findings reveal that traditional static models outperform BERT in certain scenarios, challenging the assumption that BERT's superior language understanding would yield better results. Our research highlights the importance of carefully selecting and comparing different language frameworks when studying semantic change.

The growth of massive quasars is influenced by the mass and spin of their central black holes, which are shaped by the effects of superradiance on ultralight bosons. By analyzing a sample of 1000 massive quasar black holes, we developed a method to estimate their spins using the properties of their host galaxies and the characteristics of their broad emission lines. Our analysis revealed that the distribution of black hole spins is skewed towards lower values, with a best-fit model indicating that the majority of the distribution falls below a spin value of 0.7. This finding is consistent with theoretical predictions and previous studies, and it sets a baseline for future observations that aim to constrain the properties of ultralight bosons.

A key aspect of retinal development is the migration of neuroblasts from the ventricular surface to the apical surface of the retina. This migration, which occurs between cell divisions, is known as interkinetic nuclear movement (IKM). Although it is widely accepted that IKM is essential for retinal development, the underlying mechanisms driving this movement are not fully understood. In this study, we used a combination of live imaging and mathematical modeling to investigate the mechanisms behind IKM in the zebrafish retina. Our findings suggest that IKM is driven by a diffusive movement of nuclei, which is influenced by the physical properties of the retina and the cell cycle duration. Our model also predicts that nuclei with longer cell cycle durations will migrate further, a hypothesis that can be experimentally tested. Furthermore, our model suggests that the speed of IKM is limited by the diffusion coefficient of nuclei, which may be affected by the physical properties of the retina. This study provides a framework for understanding the mechanisms behind IKM and its role in retinal development.

Code improvements for a source separation task in RGB images enable a model trained on encoded data to successfully guide a standard color demosaicing algorithm, resulting in higher quality reconstructed images.

This article investigates an Anderson-type model in the context of an incompressible polar fluid with a fixed random potential distribution on a $d$-dimensional integer lattice. The model consists of $N$ distinguishable particles, each with a specific type associated with a position and a random potential value. The system's statistical behavior is described by a grand canonical measure, and we examine its canonical version with a fixed number of particles. The system's particle count is shown to be stochastically bounded and exhibits polynomial growth in relation to the number of dimensions and the available space. Additionally, the system's specific heat is shown to be bounded for a certain range of available space.
